questions.q: Explain how the definite integral $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is defined as a limit of Riemann sums, and write the limit expression using sigma notation.
questions.target: Sums as limits: the definite integral
questions.answer: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(x_i^*)\Delta x$, where $\Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_i^*$ is any sample point in the $i$-th subinterval — as $n\rightarrow\infty$ (subintervals shrink to zero width), all Riemann sum types (left, right, midpoint) converge to the same value, the exact signed area under $f$.
questions.explanation: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(x_i^*)\Delta x$, where $\Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_i^*$ is any sample point in the $i$-th subinterval — as $n\rightarrow\infty$ (subintervals shrink to zero width), all Riemann sum types (left, right, midpoint) converge to the same value, the exact signed area under $f$.

questions.q: Determine whether the Left Riemann Sum overestimates or underestimates $\int_0^4 x^2\,dx$, and explain why using the shape of the graph.

questions.answer: Since $f(x)=x^2$ is increasing on $[0,4]$, the left endpoint of each subinterval gives the smallest function value on that subinterval, so the Left Riemann Sum UNDERESTIMATES the true area (confirmed: $L_4=14 < \frac{64}{3}\approx21.33$).
questions.explanation: Since $f(x)=x^2$ is increasing on $[0,4]$, the left endpoint of each subinterval gives the smallest function value on that subinterval, so the Left Riemann Sum UNDERESTIMATES the true area (confirmed: $L_4=14 < \frac{64}{3}\approx21.33$).

questions.q: Level 1 · Foundations Find the exact sum of the infinite geometric series: $\sum_{n=1}^\infty 3 \left( -\frac{2}{5} \right)^n$
questions.target: Riemann sums from a table of values
questions.answer: Identify the first term and ratio: When $n = 1$, $a = 3\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)^1 = -\frac{6}{5}$. The common ratio is $r = -\frac{2}{5}$. Since $|r| = \frac{2}{5} < 1$, the series converges. Using the sum formula $S = \frac{a}{1 - r}$: $S = \frac{-6/5}{1 - (-2/5)} = \frac{-6/5}{7/5} = -\frac{6}{7}$
questions.explanation: Identify the first term and ratio: When $n = 1$, $a = 3\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)^1 = -\frac{6}{5}$. The common ratio is $r = -\frac{2}{5}$. Since $|r| = \frac{2}{5} < 1$, the series converges. Using the sum formula $S = \frac{a}{1 - r}$: $S = \frac{-6/5}{1 - (-2/5)} = \frac{-6/5}{7/5} = -\frac{6}{7}$

questions.q: Level 1 · FoundationsExpress the infinite summation limit as a definite integral on the interval $[0, 1]$ and evaluate it: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i^3}{n^4}.$
questions.target: Antiderivatives of trigonometric and exponential functions
questions.answer: Factor $\frac{1}{n} = \Delta x$: $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i^3}{n^4} = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^3 \cdot \frac{1}{n}.$ Here $x_i = \frac{i}{n} = 0 + i\Delta x$ with $\Delta x = \frac{1}{n}$, matching the right Riemann sum of $f(x) = x^3$ on $[0, 1]$: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^3 \frac{1}{n} = \int_0^1 x^3\,dx = \left[ \frac{x^4}{4} \right]_0^1 = \frac{1^4}{4} - 0 = \mathbf{\frac{1}{4}}.$
questions.explanation: Factor $\frac{1}{n} = \Delta x$: $\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{i^3}{n^4} = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^3 \cdot \frac{1}{n}.$ Here $x_i = \frac{i}{n} = 0 + i\Delta x$ with $\Delta x = \frac{1}{n}$, matching the right Riemann sum of $f(x) = x^3$ on $[0, 1]$: $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{i}{n}\right)^3 \frac{1}{n} = \int_0^1 x^3\,dx = \left[ \frac{x^4}{4} \right]_0^1 = \frac{1^4}{4} - 0 = \mathbf{\frac{1}{4}}.$

questions.q: Level 2 · Medium Evaluate the indefinite integral using partial fraction decomposition: $\int \frac{5x - 3}{x^2 - 2x - 3}\,dx$
questions.target: An applied antiderivative problem
questions.cross_lesson: 8.02 Volumes by the Disc and Washer Methods
questions.answer: Factor the denominator: $x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x - 3)(x + 1)$. Set up partial fractions: $\frac{5x - 3}{(x - 3)(x + 1)} = \frac{A}{x - 3} + \frac{B}{x + 1} \Rightarrow 5x - 3 = A(x + 1) + B(x - 3)$ Using Heaviside cover-up: Set $x = 3$: $5(3) - 3 = A(3 + 1) \Rightarrow 12 = 4A \Rightarrow A = 3$. Set $x = -1$: $5(-1) - 3 = B(-1 - 3) \Rightarrow -8 = -4B \Rightarrow B = 2$. Integrate term-by-term: $\int \left( \frac{3}{x - 3} + \frac{2}{x + 1} \right)dx = 3\ln|x - 3| + 2\ln|x + 1| + C = \ln\left(|x - 3|^3 (x + 1)^2\right) + C$
questions.explanation: Factor the denominator: $x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x - 3)(x + 1)$. Set up partial fractions: $\frac{5x - 3}{(x - 3)(x + 1)} = \frac{A}{x - 3} + \frac{B}{x + 1} \Rightarrow 5x - 3 = A(x + 1) + B(x - 3)$ Using Heaviside cover-up: Set $x = 3$: $5(3) - 3 = A(3 + 1) \Rightarrow 12 = 4A \Rightarrow A = 3$. Set $x = -1$: $5(-1) - 3 = B(-1 - 3) \Rightarrow -8 = -4B \Rightarrow B = 2$. Integrate term-by-term: $\int \left( \frac{3}{x - 3} + \frac{2}{x + 1} \right)dx = 3\ln|x - 3| + 2\ln|x + 1| + C = \ln\left(|x - 3|^3 (x + 1)^2\right) + C$

questions.q: Level 2 · Medium Determine whether the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{\sqrt{n}}$ converges absolutely, converges conditionally, or diverges.
questions.target: More antiderivative practice
questions.answer: Step 1: Test for absolute convergence. Consider $\sum |a_n| = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^{1/2}}$. This is a $p$-series with $p = 1/2 \leq 1$, which diverges. Hence the series does NOT converge absolutely. Step 2: Apply Alternating Series Test. Here $b_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} > 0$. 1. Monotonicity: \(n+1 > n \implies \sqrt{n+1} > \sqrt{n} \implies \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1}} conditionally convergent.

questions.q: Does $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(0.9)^{n}$ converge, and to what?
questions.target: Comparing Riemann sums to the exact integral
questions.cross_lesson: 1.02 Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem
questions.answer: Method · Geometric Series Convergence & Sum: Step 1 · Identify series parameters: Initial term: $a = (0.9)^0 = 1$. Common ratio: $r = 0.9 = \frac{9}{10}$. Step 2 · Test convergence: $|r| = 0.9 < 1$, therefore the series converges. Step 3 · Calculate exact sum: $S = \frac{a}{1 - r} = \frac{1}{1 - 0.9} = \frac{1}{0.1} = \mathbf{10}.$ Conclusion: $\mathbf{\mathrm{Converges\ to\ } 10}$.
questions.explanation: Method · Geometric Series Convergence & Sum: Step 1 · Identify series parameters: Initial term: $a = (0.9)^0 = 1$. Common ratio: $r = 0.9 = \frac{9}{10}$. Step 2 · Test convergence: $|r| = 0.9 < 1$, therefore the series converges. Step 3 · Calculate exact sum: $S = \frac{a}{1 - r} = \frac{1}{1 - 0.9} = \frac{1}{0.1} = \mathbf{10}.$ Conclusion: $\mathbf{\mathrm{Converges\ to\ } 10}$.

questions.q: Consider the function $f(x) = \frac{\sin(2x)}{\cos(x)}$. For the domain $x \in [0, 2\pi]$ such that $\cos(x) eq 0$, find the exact value of the definite integral $\int_{0}^{\pi/2} f(x) dx$.
questions.target: Visualizing a Riemann sum approximation
questions.answer: First, we simplify the function $f(x)$. Using the double angle identity for sine, $\sin(2x) = 2\sin(x)\cos(x)$. Therefore, $f(x) = \frac{2\sin(x)\cos(x)}{\cos(x)}$. For $\cos(x) eq 0$, we can cancel the $\cos(x)$ terms, so $f(x) = 2\sin(x)$. Now we need to evaluate the definite integral: $\int_{0}^{\pi/2} 2\sin(x) dx$. The antiderivative of $2\sin(x)$ is $-2\cos(x)$. Evaluating the definite integral using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: $[-2\cos(x)]_{0}^{\pi/2} = -2\cos(\pi/2) - (-2\cos(0))$ $= -2(0) - (-2(1))$ $= 0 - (-2)$ $= 2$ Thus, the exact value of the definite integral is 2.
questions.explanation: First, we simplify the function $f(x)$. Using the double angle identity for sine, $\sin(2x) = 2\sin(x)\cos(x)$. Therefore, $f(x) = \frac{2\sin(x)\cos(x)}{\cos(x)}$. For $\cos(x) eq 0$, we can cancel the $\cos(x)$ terms, so $f(x) = 2\sin(x)$. Now we need to evaluate the definite integral: $\int_{0}^{\pi/2} 2\sin(x) dx$. The antiderivative of $2\sin(x)$ is $-2\cos(x)$. Evaluating the definite integral using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: $[-2\cos(x)]_{0}^{\pi/2} = -2\cos(\pi/2) - (-2\cos(0))$ $= -2(0) - (-2(1))$ $= 0 - (-2)$ $= 2$ Thus, the exact value of the definite integral is 2.

questions.q: Consider the power series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n (x-a)^n$. If the radius of convergence is $R=3$ and the center of the series is $a=2$, which of the following intervals represents the values of $x$ for which the series converges?
questions.target: Riemann sums: left, right, and midpoint
questions.answer: The radius of convergence $R$ of a power series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n (x-a)^n$ indicates that the series converges absolutely for $|x-a| R$. The center of the series is $a$. In this problem, we are given $R=3$ and $a=2$. Thus, the series converges for $|x-2| < 3$. This inequality can be rewritten as $-3 < x-2 < 3$. Adding 2 to all parts of the inequality, we get $-3+2 < x < 3+2$, which simplifies to $-1 < x < 5$. This interval is written in open interval notation as $(-1, 5)$. The convergence at the endpoints $x=-1$ and $x=5$ is not determined by the radius of convergence alone and requires further testing (e.g., using the Alternating Series Test or p-series test). However, the question asks for the interval where the series converges, and the open interval derived from $|x-a| < R$ is the fundamental region of convergence for a power series. Therefore, the interval $(-1, 5)$ represents the values of $x$ for which the series converges.
questions.explanation: The radius of convergence $R$ of a power series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n (x-a)^n$ indicates that the series converges absolutely for $|x-a| R$. The center of the series is $a$. In this problem, we are given $R=3$ and $a=2$. Thus, the series converges for $|x-2| < 3$. This inequality can be rewritten as $-3 < x-2 < 3$. Adding 2 to all parts of the inequality, we get $-3+2 < x < 3+2$, which simplifies to $-1 < x < 5$. This interval is written in open interval notation as $(-1, 5)$. The convergence at the endpoints $x=-1$ and $x=5$ is not determined by the radius of convergence alone and requires further testing (e.g., using the Alternating Series Test or p-series test). However, the question asks for the interval where the series converges, and the open interval derived from $|x-a| < R$ is the fundamental region of convergence for a power series. Therefore, the interval $(-1, 5)$ represents the values of $x$ for which the series converges.

questions.q: Consider the region bounded by the curves $y = x^2$ and $y = 4$. This region is revolved around the line $y = 5$ to form a solid. A cylindrical hole is drilled through the center of this solid, perpendicular to the axis of revolution. The radius of the cylindrical hole is $r$. The volume of the material removed by the cylindrical hole is given by $V_{\mathrm{hole}} = \pi \int_a^b (R(x)^2 - r^2) dx$, where $R(x)$ is the outer radius of the solid at a given $x$ and $a, b$ are the limits of integration. Find the value of $a$ and $b$, and the expression for $V_{\mathrm{hole}}$ in terms of $r$. The question asks for the setup of the integral representing the volume of the material removed.
questions.target: The Trapezoidal Rule
choices: Limits of integration are -2 and 2; $V_{\mathrm{hole}} = \pi \int_{-2}^2 ((5 - x^2)^2 - r^2) dx$
Limits of integration are 0 and 4; $V_{\mathrm{hole}} = \pi \int_{0}^4 ((4 - x^2)^2 - r^2) dx$
Limits of integration are 1 and 4; $V_{\mathrm{hole}} = \pi \int_{1}^4 ((5 - x^2)^2 - r^2) dx$
Limits of integration are -2 and 2; $V_{\mathrm{hole}} = \pi \int_{-2}^2 ((4 - x^2)^2 - r^2) dx$
questions.answer: The region is bounded by $y = x^2$ and $y = 4$. To find the intersection points, we set $x^2 = 4$, which gives $x = \pm 2$. These are our limits of integration, $a = -2$ and $b = 2$. The region is revolved around the line $y = 5$. The outer radius $R(x)$ is the distance from the axis of revolution ($y=5$) to the outer boundary of the region. The outer boundary is the curve $y = x^2$. So, $R(x) = 5 - x^2$. The inner radius of the cylindrical hole is given as $r$. The volume of the material removed by the cylindrical hole is the integral of the area of the annular cross-section, which is $\pi (R(x)^2 - r^2)$. Therefore, $V_{\mathrm{hole}} = \pi \int_{-2}^2 ((5 - x^2)^2 - r^2) dx$.

questions.q: The graph of the function $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$ is shown below. What is the definite integral of $f(x)$ from $x=1$ to $x=3$?
questions.target: Sums as limits: the definite integral
questions.answer: To find the definite integral of $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$ from $x=1$ to $x=3$, we evaluate $\int_{1}^{3} (x^2 - 4x + 3) \, dx$. First, find the antiderivative of $f(x)$: $F(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{4x^2}{2} + 3x = \frac{x^3}{3} - 2x^2 + 3x$. Next, apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: $F(3) - F(1)$. Calculate $F(3)$: $F(3) = \frac{3^3}{3} - 2(3)^2 + 3(3) = \frac{27}{3} - 2(9) + 9 = 9 - 18 + 9 = 0$. Calculate $F(1)$: $F(1) = \frac{1^3}{3} - 2(1)^2 + 3(1) = \frac{1}{3} - 2 + 3 = \frac{1}{3} + 1 = \frac{4}{3}$. Finally, subtract $F(1)$ from $F(3)$: $F(3) - F(1) = 0 - \frac{4}{3} = -\frac{4}{3}$.

questions.q: Consider the power series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(2x-1)^n}{n \cdot 3^n}$. For what values of $x$ does this series converge conditionally?
questions.target: Riemann sums from a table of values
questions.answer: Let the given power series be $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$, where $a_n = \frac{(2x-1)^n}{n \cdot 3^n}$. We will use the Ratio Test to find the interval of convergence. $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left| \frac{(2x-1)^{n+1}}{(n+1) \cdot 3^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{n \cdot 3^n}{(2x-1)^n} \right|$ $= \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left| \frac{(2x-1) \cdot n}{(n+1) \cdot 3} \right| = \left| \frac{2x-1}{3} \right| \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{n}{n+1} = \left| \frac{2x-1}{3} \right| \cdot 1 For convergence, we require this limit to be less than 1: \left| \frac{2x-1}{3} \right| < 1$ $-1 < \frac{2x-1}{3} < 1$ $-3 < 2x-1 < 3$ $-2 < 2x < 4$ $-1 < x < 2$ Now, we must check the endpoints of this interval for conditional convergence. Case 1: $x = -1$ The series becomes $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(2(-1)-1)^n}{n \cdot 3^n} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-3)^n}{n \cdot 3^n} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$. This is the alternating harmonic series, which converges conditionally by the Alternating Series Test (the terms $\frac{1}{n}$ are positive, decreasing, and tend to 0). Therefore, $x=-1$ is a point of conditional convergence. Case 2: $x = 2$ The series becomes $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(2(2)-1)^n}{n \cdot 3^n} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(3)^n}{n \cdot 3^n} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n}$. This is the harmonic series, which diverges. Thus, the series converges for $-1 \leq x < 2$. For conditional convergence, we exclude the endpoint $x=2$ where the series diverges, and include $x=-1$ where it converges conditionally. So, the interval of conditional convergence is $-1 \leq x < 2$. Common Pitfall: Forgetting to test the endpoints for convergence, or misapplying convergence tests at the endpoints. Students might incorrectly assume convergence at $x=2$ or miss conditional convergence at $x=-1$.
